paragraphs: Advocates of immersion schooling in a minority language usually argue that children who study in the language will go on to speak it at home and thereby save it from disappearance. The record is mixed. In several regions, immersion pupils became fluent yet spoke the majority language with their friends and, later, with their own children, so the minority language survived mainly inside classrooms. Critics conclude from such cases that schooling is irrelevant to revival. That conclusion is too hasty. Schools can supply speakers, but speakers will use a language only where it has some purpose outside the school gates, and where employers, shops and media operate entirely in the majority tongue that purpose is missing. Immersion education is therefore best regarded as necessary but not sufficient: it creates the pool of speakers on which revival depends, but it succeeds only when paired with public settings in which those speakers have reason to use the language.
